title: Court Halts $1.8 Billion 'Anti-Weaponization' Fund as Primaries Heat Up
summary: The Justice Department will comply with a federal court order freezing a nearly $1.8 billion fund designed to compensate people who claim they were targeted by the federal government, a program that has drawn sharp bipartisan criticism. The so-called anti-weaponization fund, a Trump administration priority, was meant to aid those alleging unfair treatment by federal agencies. But critics—including some Republicans—warned it could be used to pay individuals convicted for their roles in the January 6, 2021, Capitol attack. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche acknowledged the court's directive during a Senate hearing last month. The pause comes as six states hold primaries Tuesday, with California and Iowa featuring the most closely watched gubernatorial contests. In California's top-two system, the leading candidates will advance regardless of party, setting up a potential Democratic showdown in the fall. Democrats view these races as crucial to their strategy for retaking Congress. The primary landscape also spotlights a growing debate over closed, single-party primaries, which critics argue limit voter choice and entrench party loyalty. Some lawmakers are pushing to open primaries to all voters, a move that could reshape the composition of Congress. In foreign policy news, President Trump claimed he secured pledges from Israel and Hezbollah to pause fighting, even as Iran suspended peace talks with the U.S. over Israel's offensive in Lebanon. The announcement followed Israeli military warnings for residents in southern Beirut to evacuate ahead of planned airstrikes. On a lighter note, tennis icon Serena Williams is returning from retirement to play doubles at the HSBC Championship in London, prompting the tournament to declare, "THE QUEEN RETURNS." And for those curious about wellness trends, NPR's "Healthy or Hype?" series examines the science behind bovine colostrum supplements, made from the first milk cows produce after giving birth, which influencers claim supports gut health.
why_it_matters: The freeze on the anti-weaponization fund touches core questions about justice and fairness—who gets labeled a victim of government overreach—and shows how courts can check executive plans, a lesson in separation of powers that affects every citizen.

background_read: The January 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol was carried out by supporters of then-President Trump trying to stop the certification of Joe Biden's election win. Hundreds were arrested and convicted; some Trump allies claimed they were unfairly targeted by the Justice Department.

The term 'weaponization of government' has been used by Trump to argue that federal agencies were used against him and his supporters, a theme that led to the creation of this fund. The court freeze highlights legal challenges to such programs.

California's 'top-two' primary system, where the two leading finishers regardless of party move on, can sometimes result in two candidates from the same party competing in November, which has sparked debate about voter choice.
Serena Williams, a 23-time Grand Slam champion who retired in 2022, is widely considered one of the greatest athletes of all time. Her return to doubles is a major sports story.

Bovine colostrum is the nutrient-rich first milk from cows after birth, and it has gained popularity among wellness influencers claiming it boosts immunity and gut health, though scientific evidence is limited.

perspectives.description: Supporters of the fund, including some Trump allies, believe it offers a necessary remedy for those they see as unfairly prosecuted by a politically motivated Justice Department, restoring a sense of justice.
Critics argue the fund could reward insurrectionists and send a dangerous message that political violence is acceptable, undermining the rule of law and accountability for the Capitol attack.

The legal challenge reflects an ongoing tension: governments often create compensation programs, but when they are tied to specific political narratives, courts must weigh whether they serve a legitimate public purpose or are simply political paybacks.

If the court permanently blocks the fund, it may force the Trump administration to seek new ways to support its base, while the ongoing primaries could shift the political landscape as voters react to such debates, influencing future legislation on justice and election security.
